definitions.definition: u_t(x,t)=∂u(x,t)/∂t, component by component. Derivatives are the usual real derivatives; a derivative not existing is assigned the total derivative convention value zero. When u is smooth on its open domain these are classical derivatives.
u_tt(x,t)=∂u_t(x,t)/∂t, component by component, with the same total derivative convention.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u(x,t), the derivative along the jth standard coordinate direction, component by component with the total derivative convention. We also write u_j when the index j is explicitly fixed.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_jj(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_j(j,x,t), with the total derivative convention. The notation u_jj with fixed j has this same meaning.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: v_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t), with the total derivative convention. With fixed j we abbreviate this by v_j.
Δu(x,t)=∑_{j=1}^n u_jj(j,x,t), the componentwise spatial Laplacian Δ_xu of the input.

e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |u_j(j,x,t)|². Here |z|²=z·z is the Euclidean norm square on ℝ^m, so the spatial sum is exactly the Frobenius square |Du|². All integrals in the proof are Lebesgue integrals, and dx denotes standard volume on ℝ^n.

binders.type: vector in ℝ^m, locally bound in the norm-square identity

definitions.definition: e_t(x,t)=∂e(x,t)/∂t, using the total derivative convention, whose classical existence and formula will be proved.
For t>0, E(t)=∫_{ℝ^n}e(x,t) dx. This finite Lebesgue integral is used only once integrability of e(·,t) at every positive time has been proved; no definition at time zero is required.

inputs.statement: n≥1 and m≥1. The map u and all its partial derivatives are smooth on ℝ^n×(0,∞); in particular, for every x∈ℝ^n, t>0 and j∈{1,…,n}, ∂_t u_j(j,x,t)=v_j(j,x,t), and for every x∈ℝ^n and t>0, e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2∑_{j=1}^n u_j(j,x,t)·v_j(j,x,t). For every t0>0, let J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊆ℝ^n and R>0 such that C⊆(−R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and every positive-order derivative of u vanishes for x∉C and r∈int J. Put Q=[−R,R]^n, whose Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n. For every r∈int J the following scalar spatial functions are continuous, zero outside C, and Lebesgue integrable: e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for each j, u_j(j,·,r)·v_j(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_jj(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r)). Their absolute integrals are finite, each bounded by a finite supremum on Q times (2R)^n. In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

Let A be a measurable space with measure μ and G a normed additive commutative group and real normed space. Let I be a type, l a countably generated filter on I, F:I→A→G, f:A→G and b:A→ℝ. If eventually along l each F(i) is μ-almost-everywhere strongly measurable, eventually along l |F(i)(x)|≤b(x) for μ-almost every x, b is μ-integrable, and for μ-almost every x the values F(i)(x) tend along l to f(x), then ∫F(i)dμ tends along l to ∫f dμ.

output.statement: For every t0>0 the finite integral E is differentiable at t0 and E'(t0)=∫_{ℝ^n}e_t(x,t0) dx.

locals.declaration: Choose C from N002 at t0.
Choose the corresponding R from N002 so C⊆(−R,R)^n.
For 0<|h|<η define F(h)(x)=(e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0))/h; for other h define F(h)(x)=0. This is total, since every t0+h in the first case is positive.
Define b(x)=B 1_Q(x), where 1_Q equals one on Q and zero off Q.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and choose C,R from N002. Put Q=[−R,R]^n, η=t0/4 and I=[t0−η,t0+η]. The elementary endpoint inequalities place I strictly inside (t0/2,3t0/2). N002 makes E a finite integral at every positive time, so its guarded definition is now available. Its density and e_t are continuous on the compact set Q×I. M008 applied there to e_t gives a finite bound; replacing it by its maximum with zero gives a nonnegative finite bound for |e_t| on Q×I.

produces.statement: There exists B0≥0 such that |e_t(x,r)|≤B0 for every x∈Q and r∈I.

argument.text: Choose B as in F001 and define F and b as in the local declarations. For any x∈Q, the scalar time section r↦e(x,r) is differentiable on I by N002, with derivative e_t(x,r). Apply M002 on the convex interval I, with derivative the linear map multiplying by e_t(x,r), whose operator norm is |e_t(x,r)|≤B. For 0<|h|<η both t0 and t0+h lie in I, so |e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0)|≤B|h|. Division by |h| gives |F(h)(x)|≤B. Outside Q, N002 gives both densities zero, since both times lie inside the common time slab. Hence |F(h)(x)|≤b(x) on all of ℝ^n. The function b is integrable: Q is measurable of finite measure (2R)^n and ∫|b|=B(2R)^n<∞. For each such h, F(h) is continuous and integrable, by N002's integrability at its two times and linearity. At each x, the definition of e_t as the classical derivative gives F(h)(x)→e_t(x,t0) as h→0 through nonzero values.

produces.statement: b is Lebesgue integrable; for all real h with 0<|h|<η, F(h) is continuous and integrable and |F(h)(x)|≤b(x) for every x∈ℝ^n. For every x∈ℝ^n, F(h)(x) tends to e_t(x,t0) as h→0 through h≠0.

argument.text: Use M001 with parameter filter the punctured neighborhood filter h→0, functions F(h), limit e_t(·,t0), and bound b. This filter is countably generated: the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k, with positive integer k, form a countable neighborhood basis. F002 supplies continuity, hence a.e. strong measurability, eventually, the everywhere dominating bound, integrability of b, and pointwise convergence. Therefore ∫F(h)→∫e_t(·,t0). For 0<|h|<η, the integrability assertions of N002 give by linearity ∫F(h)=(E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. The limit is exactly the derivative criterion for E at the interior time t0, so E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0) dx. This is the derivative of the actual finite energy, not just a formal integral expression. Arbitrary t0 proves the asserted differentiated-integral formula.
